Key points:
- Initially considered a show business career but enrolled at Fordham University in 1964 to stay close to home.  
- Participated in ROTC during first year, wore a military uniform every Wednesday, but dropped ROTC in the second year.  
- Dropped football after three or four weeks; was a mediocre squash and tennis player.  
- Fordham friends introduced him to golf.  
- Transferred to the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania in his junior year; often commuted to his father's office on weekends.  
- Graduated in May 1968 with a Bachelor of Science in economics.  
- Not the top student in college and not listed among Wharton honors recipients.  
- By Wharton, he was eyeing a career in real estate.  
- Exempted from the Vietnam War draft due to bone spurs in his heels.  
- Despite five years in military school, he had no interest in going to war.

Article title: "World War II".

Key points:
- December 1941: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor and other Allied territories; United States enters the war against Japan and Germany.
- Japan conquers much of coastal China and Southeast Asia.
- June 1942: Japanese advances in the Pacific halted at the Battle of Midway.
- Early 1943: Axis defeated in North Africa and at Stalingrad (Soviet Union).
- 1943: Axis defeats on the Eastern Front; Allied invasion of Sicily and mainland Italy leads to the fall of Fascist Italy.
- Allied offensives in the Pacific push the Axis into retreat on all fronts.
- 1944: Western Allies invade France at Normandy; Soviet Union recaptures pre-war territory; United States cripples Japan’s navy and captures key Pacific islands.
- 1945 (Europe): liberation of German-occupied territories; invasions of Germany by Western Allies and Soviets; fall of Berlin; German surrender on May 8.
- 1945: Atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima (Aug 6) and Nagasaki (Aug 9); Japan announces surrender (Aug 15) and signs formal surrender (Sept 2).

Key points:

- The 1964 Liber Usualis continues to be used locally where permission exists for celebrations according to the vetus ordo.

Key points:
- Non-competitive (insurmountable) antagonists reduce the maximal response obtainable by any amount of agonist.

- In functional assays, they depress the maximal agonist response; sometimes produce rightward shifts.
- Rightward shift can occur due to receptor reserve (spare receptors); inhibition occurs only when this reserve is depleted.
- Unlike competitive antagonists, which affect potency (EC50) but not the maximal response, non-competitive antagonists reduce the maximal response (Emax).

Article title: "Lithic flake".

Key points:
- Striking platform: the proximal point where the detachment blow or pressure occurred; can be natural or prepared. 
- Termination type: describes how the distal end detached from the core. 
- Flake terminations: feathered, hinged, stepped, or plunging (overshot/outrepassé). 
- Feathered terminations: very sharp; flake thins gradually before force exits the core. 
- Hinged terminations: force rolls away from the core; distal end becomes rounded. 
- Stepped terminations: flake breaks or snaps during removal; distal end often squared off. 
- Plunging terminations: force rolls back toward the core; may take off its bottom. 
- Abrupt terminations: hinge, step, and plunging terminations; can be deliberate but usually errors; indicate internal core flaws or prior Hertzian cones. 
- Eraillures (bulbar scars): tiny flake scars on bulbs of applied force; cause not fully understood. 
- Among flakes with eraillures, very few exhibit more than one.

- Vowels /i/ and /u/ are shown by diacritics placed above (for /i/) or below (for /u/) the consonant letter.
- Lone vowels have independent letters for /a/, /i/, and /u/ (three letters in total).
- Syllables ending in a consonant are written without the final consonant.
- Tagbanwa differs from Baybayin in the shapes of several letters, notably ka and wa, which are markedly different.
